title: Phishing Detector Extension
content:
I built a browser extension that uses a Random Forest model to detect phishing websites. It scans webpage features in real time and warns users of suspicious activity.

The model was trained on a labeled dataset and deployed inside the extension using WebExtension APIs.

Tech used: Python, scikit-learn, JavaScript.

title: Kaggle Titanic Survival Prediction
content:
This project was my introduction to supervised machine learning. I explored the Titanic dataset and built classification models to predict passenger survival.

I applied feature engineering, handled missing values, and evaluated logistic regression, decision trees, and SVMs.

Tools: Pandas, Scikit-Learn, Matplotlib.

title: Blue Girl: A Love Story?? Nope. I Failed Calculus.
content:
There I stood, frozen outside Room 24, mentally calculating the weight of my Calculus 2 exam failure—specifically, how many disappointed sighs my dad could fit into one phone call. I was Googling ‘Can a GPA file for bankruptcy?’ when fate decided to mess with me one more time.

Enter: Blue Girl.

She didn’t walk up. She appeared. No footsteps. No stair creaks. Just—boom. Human anomaly. She looked like someone who knew exactly what office she was going to and also exactly how to ruin my ability to form coherent thoughts.

My brain? Blue-screened. Like, actual mental 404. At that moment, I forgot about limits, derivatives, and my own first name. (Fun fact: When you fail a math exam, the universe sometimes sends an unexpected variable. In this case, the variable was ‘X = why am I sweating through my shirt?’)

Nigel, my academic comrade-in-suffering, was there too. We’d both been flayed alive by the same partial derivative demon, so we were bonded. Trauma twins. She said something—I think. I responded, maybe? All I remember is stammering like a Wi-Fi signal in a thunderstorm: ‘So, uh… I’m in 400… I mean… haha yeah…you…’ Smooth as sandpaper.

And then—she took my number.

Let me repeat that. *She*. Took. *My number.*

Exactly how I imagined meeting The One™️—emerging like a Marvel origin story. Except instead of superpowers, we shared the mutual academic skillset of a confused toaster. The universe’s equation? -1 calculus grade + 1 inexplicably glowing human in blue = net emotional gain (but still a tragic GPA).

P.S. Dr. Ansong, if you ever read this: Please consider banning partial derivatives. For the culture.

title: HR 1 : 0 Me
content:
So it turns out—surprise!—that to pass an interview, you need to do more than just answer the questions. Apparently, it’s not about raw honesty, it’s about flair. Confidence. A bit of charm. Basically: interviews are less like exams and more like trying to flirt with HR.

Now, listen—I can’t flirt. I barely make eye contact with a girl. And there I was, trapped in an online interview, and to make matters worse: the interviewer was a woman. That's two of my weaknesses in one neat little Zoom window. If this were a Pokémon battle, I was up against a type I’m tragically weak to.

She asked, ‘What inspired you to pursue computer science?’ I panicked. I wanted to say ‘money’—because, let’s be honest—but I knew that wouldn’t get me the job. Apparently, I was supposed to say something like, ‘I’ve always had a passion for solving real-world problems.’

Who told employers that everyone loves solving problems?? I want to get paid. That’s the problem I’m trying to solve! Poverty (Notice the caital p?? It feels uneccessary to point that out but I just had to emphasize the capital just so you don't overlook it.)

Anyway, leave it to me to fumble, I wont disappoint.

The worst part? I had practiced. I had flashcards. I even had a ‘Tell me about yourself?’ monologue that made me sound like I ran a startup in my garage. But the moment the camera turned on, my brain turned off.

Needless to say, I did not get the job.

Next time? Oh, I’m lying. I will lie so hard my ancestors will feel it. I’ll say I was hacking toy robots at age 6, that I helped redesign the school’s network infrastructure in JSS3, that I taught Java to my dog. You want flair? I’ll give you fireworks.

P.S. If you’re reading this and you're an interviewer: please just hire people based on vibes. My vibes are great. My answers? Not so much.

title: Predicting Optimal Fertilizers-Kaggle Competition
content:
I’ll be honest—I’ve always hated hackathons and competitions. There’s something about the pressure and the leaderboard that makes me feel like an impostor. But this time, I decided to dive into a Kaggle competition anyway. After all, how else would I learn?

Scrolling through Kaggle’s endless list of challenges, one title caught my eye: Predicting Optimal Fertilizers. A classification problem? Perfect. My last attempt at a competition (shoutout to Zindi, where I crashed and burned) taught me one thing: winning isn’t about reinventing the wheel—it’s about finetuning better than everyone else.

So, I rolled up my sleeves. My plan? Pit two heavyweight models against each other—LightGBM and XGBoost—then merge their strengths into a Frankenstein’s monster of a hybrid model. Because if one model is good, two must be better, right? (Famous last words.)

And the results? I placed 1007th out of 2379. That means I outperformed about 58% of the competition. Not podium-worthy, but hey, I’ll take ‘above average’ over total embarrassment any day.

Also, just in time for a comeback arc—the next Zindi hackathon kicks off on July 5th. Maybe this time I will outperform 80%. No promises, though.

P.S. If anyone knows how to actually win these things, my DMs are wide open.

title: Zindi Yango Hackathon
content:
So I did another one—Zindi hackathon #2. This time, we were asked to do something truly ambitious: predict taxi ride times in Accra using weather and trip data. Basically, become a digital prophet of chaos. Have you seen Accra traffic?? Not even Google Maps dares to be too confident.

Anyway, I joined. Again. Because apparently, I like pain.

The dataset was a mix of trip start times, routes, and weather conditions (because obviously, rain = extra suffering). I have to build a model that could somehow understand what even the drivers don’t: how long it would take to go from A to B without the gods of traffic messing everything up.

I played around with Random Forest and Gradient Boosting. Even tried to normalize timestamps like I knew what I was doing. I don’t know who needs to hear this, but: feature engineering is just guesswork in a lab coat.

Final result? I placed 39th out of 92 participants. That’s better than half. Not amazing, but definitely not trash. That puts me in the ‘I tried’ zone—which is my comfort zone, honestly.

My takeaway? Predicting taxi times is hard. Predicting Zindi leaderboard positions? Even harder. But I’m getting better. Slowly. And with more all nighters and caffeine.

P.S. Shoutout to my partner and 'Akonta' (brother in-law) Jones Adu Asamoah. We worked as a team. Link to the certificate

title: Building an OOH Monitoring System for Dentsu
content:
On 3rd September, 2025. I took on a freelance contract to build a real-time Out-Of-Home (OOH) Monitoring and Analytics System for Dentsu — one of the world’s largest advertising and media companies.

The goal was to give Dentsu and its clients live visibility into their outdoor campaigns — tracking board conditions, impressions, competitor presence, and performance across Ghana. The system I built, internally called BaudCOM, became a hub for campaign transparency and operational efficiency.

⚙️ The Challenge

The project needed to:

  • Display a live dashboard showing each board’s location, condition, and spend.
  • Provide competitive benchmarking (Share of Voice by road and brand).
  • Send automated alerts when boards were torn, fixed, or fully flighted.
  • Allow batch editing of boards and generate PDF/CSV reports.
  • Handle large CSV-based data ingestion from field updates.

💻 Tech Stack

  • Backend: Node.js + Express
  • Templating: EJS (for fast SSR rendering)
  • Database: CSV + XLSX persistence (atomic file writes)
  • Automation: Node-cron (scheduled alert jobs)
  • Reports: PDFKit + CSV exports
  • Styling: TailwindCSS
  • Charts: Chart.js for visual analytics

🚀 My Key Contributions

  • Live KPI Dashboard — built clickable KPI cards that filter boards in real time (e.g., view only 'Poor' or 'Critical' boards).
  • Competitor Analytics — implemented Share of Voice visualizations limited to the Top 10 roads for clarity and speed.
  • Email Alerts System — automated notifications for torn/fixed boards and campaign flighting completion.
  • Batch Editing — allowed admins to modify multiple records simultaneously, improving workflow efficiency.
  • SEO Optimization — added meta tags, Open Graph, and canonical links for better Google ranking.

🧠 Technical Highlights

  • Used atomic file saving (temp → rename) to ensure data consistency in flat-file persistence.
  • Optimized query filtering and pagination to maintain state across brand and agent filters.
  • Designed idempotent cron jobs — safe to re-run without duplicate alerts.
  • Handled real-time reporting and brand-based user access control using JWT authentication.

🏁 Outcome

The platform gave Dentsu’s media teams and clients real-time campaign visibility for the first time — replacing spreadsheets and manual updates with automated insights and alerts.

It streamlined OOH operations, improved accountability, and demonstrated how software can modernize traditional advertising workflows.

💡 Lessons Learned

  • Always validate sample data early — data inconsistencies break everything later.
  • Make filters URL-driven so they persist across pagination and reloads.
  • Use atomic file operations for safe updates when working without a DB.
  • Build modular automation: cron jobs, alerts, and exports should scale independently.

Built under a freelance contract for Dentsu. © 2025 BaudCOM Project — by Adenutsi Andy Eleos.
